candidates.topic: The Cicada 13-Year and 17-Year Prime Number Emergence
candidates.teaser: Cicadas count prime numbers — and scientists still can't fully explain why.
candidates.video_title: Cicadas Can Count Prime Numbers (Scientists Are Baffled)
candidates.video_description: Periodical cicadas emerge in exact 13- or 17-year cycles — both prime numbers. This mathematical precision in an insect's biology has puzzled evolutionary biologists for decades, and the leading theory is stranger than fiction.
candidates.script: Billions of insects just vanished underground — and they set an alarm for exactly 17 years. Periodical cicadas emerge in cycles of either 13 or 17 years. Both prime numbers. No exceptions. Scientists believe they evolved this to outsmart predators — because no predator breeds on a 13 or 17-year cycle, they always catch prey off guard. An insect that never learned math somehow solved a problem mathematicians study. Does that change how you think about intelligence?

candidates.topic: The Sediment Slab — Earthquake That Reversed the Mississippi River
candidates.teaser: An earthquake once made one of the world's mightiest rivers run backwards — for three days.
candidates.video_title: The Earthquake That Reversed the Mississippi River
candidates.video_description: In 1811, the New Madrid earthquake was so powerful it temporarily reversed the flow of the Mississippi River, created new lakes overnight, and rang church bells as far away as Boston. It remains the most powerful earthquake ever recorded in North America.
candidates.script: For three days in 1811, the Mississippi River flowed backwards. The New Madrid earthquake — magnitude estimated at 8.1 — buckled the land so violently that the river reversed course, swallowed entire forests, and created Reelfoot Lake overnight. Church bells rang on their own in Boston, 1,500 miles away. It remains the most powerful earthquake in recorded North American history — and it happened nowhere near a tectonic plate boundary. Could it happen again today?

candidates.topic: The Woman Who Can Smell Parkinson's Disease
candidates.teaser: A Scottish woman detected a disease through smell alone — years before doctors could using any test.
candidates.video_title: She Smelled Parkinson's Disease Before Doctors Could Detect It
candidates.video_description: Joy Milne, a retired nurse from Scotland, noticed her husband smelled different years before his Parkinson's diagnosis. Scientists tested her ability and she correctly identified 12 out of 12 Parkinson's patients by scent alone — then identified a 13th patient who hadn't yet been diagnosed.
candidates.script: She told her husband he smelled different. Six years later, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. Joy Milne, a Scottish nurse, could smell the illness before any medical test could find it. Scientists gave her 12 unlabeled shirts — she identified every Parkinson's patient correctly. Then flagged a 13th person as positive. That person had no diagnosis. Eight months later, doctors confirmed he had Parkinson's. Her nose led to the discovery of a real biomarker — a musky odor on the skin. What else are we missing?

candidates.topic: The Ship That Sank Twice — AHS Centaur
candidates.teaser: A hospital ship was sunk illegally in WWII — and one survivor's story made it even more unbelievable.
candidates.video_title: The Hospital Ship Sunk Illegally — One Survivor's Impossible Story
candidates.video_description: In 1943, the AHS Centaur was clearly marked as a hospital ship under the Geneva Convention, yet was torpedoed by a Japanese submarine off Australia. Of 332 people on board, only 64 survived — including one nurse who stayed afloat for 35 hours clinging to wreckage.
candidates.script: It was painted white with giant red crosses. Every international law protected it. The Japanese submarine torpedoed it anyway. The AHS Centaur, a WWII hospital ship, sank in 33 minutes off the coast of Australia in 1943. Of 332 people on board, 268 died. One nurse — Sister Ellen Savage — survived 35 hours alone in shark-filled waters with broken ribs and a ruptured eardrum. She was still tending to other survivors when rescuers arrived. What do you call that?

candidates.topic: The Bone Wars — Victorian Paleontologists Who Sabotaged Each Other
candidates.teaser: Two scientists destroyed each other's careers, reputations, and digs — but accidentally gave us most of what we know about dinosaurs.
candidates.video_title: The Rivalry That Discovered Most of America's Dinosaurs
candidates.video_description: Othniel Marsh and Edward Cope began as friends and ended as obsessive enemies, dynamiting each other's fossil sites, publishing fake discoveries, and spying on one another for over 20 years. Their destructive rivalry — known as the Bone Wars — produced 142 new dinosaur species.
candidates.script: They dynamited each other's dig sites so the enemy couldn't use them. Othniel Marsh and Edward Cope started as friends in the 1870s, then spent 20 years in a savage war over fossils — bribing workers, publishing fake findings, and mailing boxes of bones just to win the count. Their obsession was irrational, vindictive, and completely ruinous for both. It also gave science 142 new dinosaur species, including Triceratops and Stegosaurus. Without their hatred — would we even know those animals existed?
